# Getting Started

@nanoviews/storybook renders Nanoviews stories in Storybook, and @nanoviews/storybook-vite runs it on the Vite builder.

`@nanoviews/storybook` is the [Storybook](https://storybook.js.org/) renderer for Nanoviews, and `@nanoviews/storybook-vite` is the framework that runs it on the Vite builder of Storybook.

- **CSF3**. Stories are plain Component Story Format objects, typed with `Meta` and `StoryObj`.
- **Args are signals**. A story's `render` is a Nanoviews component that receives the args as writable signals, so an edited control updates the view in place, with no remount.
- **Portable stories**. `composeStories` turns stories into functions that `@nanoviews/testing-library` renders in unit tests.
- **One option**. A single `framework` entry in `.storybook/main.ts` wires the renderer to the Vite builder.

## Renderer and Framework

Storybook integrates a view library through two kinds of packages. `@nanoviews/storybook` is the *renderer*: it teaches Storybook how to mount and update a Nanoviews tree. It has no builder of its own, so it needs a *framework*: `@nanoviews/storybook-vite` wires it to [`@storybook/builder-vite`](https://storybook.js.org/docs/builders/vite).

The framework depends on the renderer and re-exports its whole API, so a project installs the framework alone and imports everything from `@nanoviews/storybook-vite`, the story API and the config types alike.

## Installation

Install the packages as dev dependencies, together with Storybook and Vite:

```bash
pnpm add -D @nanoviews/storybook-vite storybook vite
```

`storybook` (10.5.10 or a later 10.x) and `vite` (5 to 8) are peer dependencies of the framework, and `nanoviews` is a peer dependency of the renderer.

## Setup

The Storybook CLI cannot scaffold a third-party framework, so the setup is done by hand: two config files and two scripts.

- .storybook/
  - main.ts the framework and the story files
  - preview\.ts global parameters, decorators and loaders
- src/
  - button.ts
  - button.stories.ts
- package.json

### `.storybook/main.ts`

```ts title=".storybook/main.ts"
import type { StorybookConfig } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'

const config: StorybookConfig = {
  framework: '@nanoviews/storybook-vite',
  stories: ['../src/**/*.stories.ts']
}

export default config
```

`framework` names the framework package. Storybook loads its preset, which sets the Vite builder and the Nanoviews renderer. `stories` lists the globs of the story files, relative to the `.storybook` directory. The object form of `framework`, `viteFinal` and `defineMain` are covered in the API.

### `.storybook/preview.ts`

Optional, but this is where global parameters, decorators and loaders live. Its default export is typed with `Preview`:

```ts title=".storybook/preview.ts"
import type { Preview } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'

const preview: Preview = {
  parameters: {
    controls: {
      matchers: {
        color: /(background|color)$/i,
        date: /Date$/i
      }
    }
  }
}

export default preview
```

The [control matchers](https://storybook.js.org/docs/essentials/controls) pick a control by the name of the arg: a color picker for the args whose names end with `background` or `color`, a date picker for the ones that end with `Date`.

### Scripts

```json title="package.json"
{
  "scripts": {
    "storybook": "storybook dev -p 6006",
    "build-storybook": "storybook build"
  }
}
```

`storybook dev` serves Storybook on port 6006 and opens it in the browser (`--no-open` skips that). `storybook build` writes a static Storybook into `storybook-static`.

## First Story

A button with an optional primary look and a click handler, which takes its label as children:

```ts title="src/button.ts"
import { type Signalish, when } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { button, component$ } from 'nanoviews'

export interface ButtonProps {
  primary?: Signalish<boolean>
  onClick?: (event: MouseEvent) => void
}

export const Button = component$(({ primary, onClick }: ButtonProps, children) => (
  button({
    class: ['button', when(primary, 'button_primary')],
    onClick
  })(
    ...children
  )
))
```

Its stories set the args, and the `render` of the meta passes the label as a child:

```ts title="src/button.stories.ts"
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { fn } from 'storybook/test'
import { Button } from './button.js'

const meta: Meta<typeof Button> = {
  title: 'Button',
  args: {
    primary: false,
    onClick: fn()
  },
  render(props) {
    return Button(props)('Send')
  }
}

export default meta

type Story = StoryObj<typeof meta>

export const Default: Story = {}
// <button class="button">Send</button>

export const Primary: Story = {
  args: {
    primary: true
  }
}
// <button class="button button_primary">Send</button>
```

The `args` of the meta apply to every story, and the `args` of a story are merged over them. `primary` is a `Signalish<boolean>` prop, so its arg is a plain boolean, and the Controls panel shows it as a toggle. The renderer hands `Button` a signal instead: a toggle is written into that signal, and the class of the same button changes. `fn()` from `storybook/test` makes a spy, which the [Actions](https://storybook.js.org/docs/essentials/actions) panel logs on every click.

Start Storybook with the `storybook` script, and both stories show up under **Button** in the sidebar.

# Writing Stories

Write CSF3 stories for Nanoviews: the Meta forms, args as writable signals, decorators and loaders.

Stories are plain [CSF3](https://storybook.js.org/docs/api/csf): a default export with the metadata and a named export per example. A story's `render` is a Nanoviews component like any other: it gets props and returns a view. The props are the story's args, each plain value wrapped in a writable signal.

## CSF3

```ts title="src/style.stories.ts"
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { div } from 'nanoviews'

const meta: Meta<{
  color: string
}> = {
  title: 'Elements/Style'
}

export default meta

type Story = StoryObj<typeof meta>

export const StaticValue: Story = {
  render() {
    return (
      div({
        style: {
          color: 'green'
        }
      })(
        'Hello, world!'
      )
    )
  }
}
// <div style="color: green;">Hello, world!</div>

export const ReactiveValue: Story = {
  args: {
    color: 'green'
  },
  // `color` here is a `WritableSignal<string>`, not a `string`
  render({ color }) {
    return (
      div({
        style: () => ({
          color: color()
        })
      })(
        'Hello, world!'
      )
    )
  }
}
// <div style="color: green;">Hello, world!</div>
```

`StaticValue` uses no args. The meta types `color` as a plain string and `ReactiveValue` sets it to `'green'`, but its `render` receives a `WritableSignal<string>`: the `style` accessor reads it, so an edit of the control restyles the same `div`. `title` places the stories in the sidebar, with `/` nesting them in groups; without it, Storybook derives the title from the file path.

## Typing the Meta

`Meta` can be parameterized either with the component or with the plain args type: the values you put into `args` and the Controls panel edits. Both forms describe the same story: `args` stays plain, `render` and the component get signals. `StoryObj<typeof meta>` types the stories after the meta.

### `Meta<typeof Component>`

The component form reads the args off the props of the component. Here it is the `Button` of Getting Started, with a story that renders it next to a second one:

```ts title="src/button-pair.stories.ts"
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { div } from 'nanoviews'
import { Button } from './button.js'

const meta: Meta<typeof Button> = {
  title: 'Button',
  component: Button,
  args: {
    label: 'Send'
  }
}

export default meta

type Story = StoryObj<typeof meta>

export const WithCancel: Story = {
  args: {
    primary: true
  },
  // label: WritableSignal<string>
  // primary: WritableSignal<boolean> | undefined
  // onClick: ((event: MouseEvent) => void) | undefined
  render({ label, primary, onClick }) {
    return (
      div()(
        Button({
          label,
          primary,
          onClick
        }),
        Button({
          label: 'Cancel'
        })
      )
    )
  }
}
// <div><button class="button button_primary">Send</button><button class="button">Cancel</button></div>
```

A prop becomes an arg this way:

| Prop of the component                          | Arg in `args` and Controls    | What `render` and the component get |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `Signalish<T>`                                 | `T`                           | `WritableSignal<T>`                 |
| `WritableSignal<T>`                            | `T`                           | `WritableSignal<T>`                 |
| a function: an event handler, an `Accessor<T>` | the function                  | the same function                   |
| optional, `name?:`                             | the same, and may be left out | the same, or `undefined`            |

A signal from `render` fits a `Signalish` prop, so `render` passes the args on to the component as they came. The renderer hands the component a signal for every arg that is not a function, so a prop typed as a plain value, like `id: string`, makes the `component` of the meta a type error: type it `Signalish<string>` instead.

> Caution: A component made with `component$` whose props are all optional takes them through an optional parameter, and `Meta<typeof Component>` cannot read the args off it: they come out untyped (`any`). Type the meta of such a component with the args form below.

### `Meta<Args>`

The args form names the plain args type itself. It fits a story that renders more than one component, a view with no component at all, and a component whose props are all optional:

```ts title="src/button-args.stories.ts"
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { Button } from './button.js'

const meta: Meta<{
  label: string
  primary?: boolean
}> = {
  title: 'Button/Args'
}

export default meta

type Story = StoryObj<typeof meta>

export const Primary: Story = {
  args: {
    label: 'Send',
    primary: true
  },
  render({ label, primary }) {
    return (
      Button({
        label,
        primary
      })
    )
  }
}
// <button class="button button_primary">Send</button>
```

## Stories Without a Render

`component` in the meta is what its stories render by default: the renderer calls it with the args, as signals. A story that only picks args needs no `render` of its own, and the `Button` stories of Getting Started are just `{}` and `{ args: { primary: true } }`. A `render` in the meta is the default `render` of every story in the module, as in the `Profile` stories [below](#optional-args).

A story with neither a `render` nor a `component` to fall back to fails to render, with `Unable to render story <id> as the component annotation is missing from the default export`.

## Args Are Signals

An arg has two ends: the story declares it as a plain value, and the view receives it as a writable signal. Everything between the two is the renderer. On the first render of a canvas it wraps every plain arg in a `signal()` and mounts the story once with that map of signals. On every next render (a control edited, the controls reset) it **writes the new plain values into the same signals** instead of passing them to a new component instance. There is no re-render: the signal updates exactly the bindings that depend on it, and the rest of the view, its state included, stays as it is.

So one prop has three shapes, and the props types name all three:

- what the story declares, in `args` and the Controls panel: plain values;
- what `render` and the component receive: writable signals;
- what a composed story accepts in a test: either of the two.

### Reading Args

`render` runs once per mount, so a value read from an arg in its body is read once. Derive from the signals with `computed`, an arrow function or an operator, or hand the signal itself to an attribute, a child or a control flow block like `if_`:

```ts title="src/total.stories.ts"
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { computed } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { p } from 'nanoviews'

const meta: Meta<{
  price: number
  quantity: number
}> = {
  title: 'Total'
}

export default meta

type Story = StoryObj<typeof meta>

export const Total: Story = {
  args: {
    price: 10,
    quantity: 2
  },
  render({ price, quantity }) {
    const $total = computed(() => price() * quantity())

    return (
      p()(
        'Total: ', $total
      )
    )
  }
}
// <p>Total: 20</p>
```

`price() * quantity()` written straight into the render body would compute `20` once and keep showing it after an edit of either control.

### Optional Args

An optional arg reaches `render` as `WritableSignal<T> | undefined`, because an arg that is left out is not passed at all:

```ts title="src/profile.stories.ts"
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { p, b, span } from 'nanoviews'

const meta: Meta<{
  name: string
  role?: string
}> = {
  title: 'Profile',
  render({ name, role }) {
    return (
      p()(
        b()(name),
        role && span()(', ', role)
      )
    )
  }
}

export default meta

type Story = StoryObj<typeof meta>

export const NameOnly: Story = {
  args: {
    name: 'Ada'
  }
}
// <p><b>Ada</b></p>

export const WithRole: Story = {
  args: {
    name: 'Ada',
    role: 'Engineer'
  }
}
// <p><b>Ada</b><span>, Engineer</span></p>
```

`role && span()(', ', role)` checks the arg once, when the story mounts: whether an arg is there is fixed for the life of the mounted view, see [What Remounts](#what-remounts).

### Function Args

Args that are functions are passed through untouched, and so are args that are already signals, like the ones a test passes to a composed story:

```ts title="src/tag.stories.ts"
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { fn } from 'storybook/test'
import { button } from 'nanoviews'

const meta: Meta<{
  label: string
  onSelect: (label: string) => void
}> = {
  title: 'Tag'
}

export default meta

type Story = StoryObj<typeof meta>

export const Selectable: Story = {
  args: {
    label: 'nanoviews',
    onSelect: fn()
  },
  // `onSelect` is the `fn()` spy itself, `label` is a signal
  render({ label, onSelect }) {
    return (
      button({
        onClick() {
          onSelect(label())
        }
      })(
        label
      )
    )
  }
}
// <button>nanoviews</button>
```

The [Actions](https://storybook.js.org/docs/essentials/actions) panel logs every call of the `fn()` spy. The click handler reads `label()` when the click happens, so it sends the label the control holds at that moment.

### What Remounts

The story is unmounted and mounted again, with fresh signals made from the current args, on:

- a change of [globals](https://storybook.js.org/docs/essentials/toolbars-and-globals): a toolbar like backgrounds, viewport, measure or outline, or one of your own `globalTypes`;
- the **Reload story** button of the toolbar.

A remount starts the view over: state that lives inside its components, like the count of a counter, is reset. The signals are made for the args the story has when it mounts, so an optional arg that was left out and is then set from the Controls panel reaches the view only at the next remount.

## Decorators

A [decorator](https://storybook.js.org/docs/writing-stories/decorators) wraps the view the story rendered, the same way as in every other Storybook renderer. Every named export of a stories file is taken for a story, so a shared decorator lives in a module of its own:

```ts title=".storybook/decorators.ts"
import type { Decorator } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { div } from 'nanoviews'

export const withPadding: Decorator = story => (
  div({
    class: 'padded'
  })(
    story()
  )
)
```

`decorators` takes it in the meta, in a story or in the preview:

```ts title="src/padded.stories.ts"
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { withPadding } from '../.storybook/decorators.js'
import { Button } from './button.js'

const meta: Meta<typeof Button> = {
  title: 'Button/Padded',
  component: Button,
  decorators: [withPadding],
  args: {
    label: 'Send'
  }
}

export default meta

type Story = StoryObj<typeof meta>

export const Default: Story = {}
// <div class="padded"><button class="button">Send</button></div>
```

Decorators run once per mount, together with the story they wrap: later arg edits reach the view through the signals, not through a new call to the decorator.

### Args in Decorators

`context.args` of a decorator holds the same signals the render gets. The `decorators` of `Meta` and `StoryObj` type it with the plain args, so hand an arg to a binding, which takes a signal and a value alike, instead of reading it as a plain value:

```ts title="src/titled.stories.ts"
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { div } from 'nanoviews'
import { Button } from './button.js'

const meta: Meta<typeof Button> = {
  title: 'Button/Titled',
  component: Button,
  decorators: [
    // typed `string`, but `args.label` is the signal the button gets
    (story, { args }) => (
      div({
        title: args.label
      })(
        story()
      )
    )
  ],
  args: {
    label: 'Send'
  }
}

export default meta

type Story = StoryObj<typeof meta>

export const Default: Story = {}
// <div title="Send"><button class="button">Send</button></div>
```

The `title` follows every edit of `label`, while the decorator itself ran once. A shared decorator that reads args is typed with the plain args too, `Decorator<{ label: string }>`, and fits the `decorators` of a meta or a story with those args.

### Globals and Dependency Injection

A change of globals [remounts](#what-remounts) the story, so a decorator that reads `context.globals` runs again on every toolbar change. A decorator is also the place to open the injection context that a component needs for `inject`: a story has none of its own. A factory for the theme:

```ts title="src/theme.ts"
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'

export type Theme = 'light' | 'dark'

export function Theme$() {
  return signal<Theme>('light')
}
```

The preview adds a theme toolbar and provides its value to every story:

```ts title=".storybook/preview.ts"
import type { Preview } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { signal, provide } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { context$ } from 'nanoviews'
import { type Theme, Theme$ } from '../src/theme.js'

const preview: Preview = {
  globalTypes: {
    theme: {
      description: 'Color theme',
      toolbar: {
        title: 'Theme',
        items: ['light', 'dark']
      }
    }
  },
  initialGlobals: {
    theme: 'light'
  },
  decorators: [
    (story, { globals }) => (
      context$(
        provide(Theme$, signal<Theme>(globals.theme))
      )(
        story()
      )
    )
  ]
}

export default preview
```

Everything a story renders gets the theme of the toolbar, its `render` included, and a story can pin one with its `globals`:

```ts title="src/themed.stories.ts"
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { inject } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { span } from 'nanoviews'
import { Theme$ } from './theme.js'

const meta: Meta = {
  title: 'Themed',
  render() {
    const $theme = inject(Theme$)

    return (
      span()(
        $theme
      )
    )
  }
}

export default meta

type Story = StoryObj<typeof meta>

export const Default: Story = {}
// <span>light</span>

export const Dark: Story = {
  globals: {
    theme: 'dark'
  }
}
// <span>dark</span>
```

`story()` hands the story back unbuilt: it renders once `context$` builds it, inside the context, the way a component renders inside its parent. So `render` can `inject` what a decorator provides, and so can a decorator inside the one that opened the context.

## Loaders

A [loader](https://storybook.js.org/docs/writing-stories/loaders) runs before the story mounts and receives the plain args. What it returns is merged into `loaded` of the story context, which `render` gets as its second argument. `fetchUser` stands for a request function of the app:

```ts title="src/user.stories.ts"
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { p } from 'nanoviews'
import { fetchUser } from './api.js'

const meta: Meta<{
  id: number
}> = {
  title: 'User'
}

export default meta

type Story = StoryObj<typeof meta>

export const Loaded: Story = {
  args: {
    id: 1
  },
  loaders: [
    async ({ args }) => ({
      user: await fetchUser(args.id)
    })
  ],
  render(_, { loaded }) {
    return p()('Hello, ', loaded.user.name)
  }
}
// <p>Hello, Ada</p>
```

The mounted view keeps the `loaded` of its first render. Storybook runs the loaders again on every arg edit, but only the new args reach the mounted view: the user fetched for a new `id` shows up at the next [remount](#what-remounts). A composed story runs its loaders when its `load()` is awaited, see Portable Stories.

---

# Portable Stories

Compose stories into functions and render them in unit tests with @nanoviews/testing-library.

`composeStories` applies the meta, the renderer and the project annotations passed to it to every story of a module, so the story becomes a function you can call in a test. Calling a composed story returns the story unbuilt, like a component instance: `render` of `@nanoviews/testing-library` takes it as it is, and a view takes it as a child, so a story goes into a test with no Storybook running. The tests on this page use Vitest, set up as in Testing.

## `composeStories`

The `Elements/Style` stories of Writing Stories, composed and rendered:

```ts title="src/style.spec.ts"
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest'
import { composeStories } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { render } from '@nanoviews/testing-library'
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import * as Stories from './style.stories.js'

const { StaticValue, ReactiveValue } = composeStories(Stories)

describe('style', () => {
  it('should render static value', () => {
    const { container } = render(StaticValue())

    expect(container.innerHTML).toBe('<div><div style="color: green;">Hello, world!</div></div>')
  })

  it('should render overridden value', () => {
    const { container } = render(ReactiveValue({
      color: 'red'
    }))

    expect(container.innerHTML).toBe('<div><div style="color: red;">Hello, world!</div></div>')
  })

  it('should render reactive value', () => {
    const $color = signal('green')
    const { container } = render(ReactiveValue({
      color: $color
    }))

    expect(container.innerHTML).toBe('<div><div style="color: green;">Hello, world!</div></div>')

    $color('red')

    expect(container.innerHTML).toBe('<div><div style="color: red;">Hello, world!</div></div>')
  })
})
```

Import the stories module as a namespace: `composeStories` takes the meta from its `default` export and composes the stories of the other exports. The extra `<div>` in `container.innerHTML` is the element the view was mounted into: `container` is `document.body`, and `render` creates the target `<div>` inside of it.

## Args

Every arg of a composed story is optional and can be passed as a plain value or as a signal. The story is reactive either way, because the renderer wraps the plain ones, and an arg left out falls back to the args of the story and its meta, wrapped in a signal just the same. Passing a signal is how you get the handle to drive the story with: write to it and assert on the DOM it changed. A function is passed through as it is, so a spy goes in as an event handler. With the `Button` stories of Getting Started:

```ts title="src/button.spec.ts"
import { it, expect, vi } from 'vitest'
import { composeStories } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from '@nanoviews/testing-library'
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import * as Stories from './button.stories.js'

const { Default, Primary } = composeStories(Stories)

it('should call onClick on click', () => {
  const onClick = vi.fn()

  render(Default({
    onClick
  }))
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button'))

  expect(onClick).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)
})

it('should follow the label signal', () => {
  const $label = signal('Send')

  render(Primary({
    label: $label
  }))
  $label('Sent')

  expect(screen.getByRole('button').textContent).toBe('Sent')
})
```

The write to `$label` updates the text before the next line runs, so the assertion needs no `await`. Each call of a composed story wraps the plain args in new signals, so two renders of one story do not share them. The `args` property of a composed story holds the args it falls back to: `Default.args.onClick` is the `fn()` spy of the meta.

## `composeStory`

To compose a single story instead of the whole module, `composeStory` takes the story and the meta of the module it comes from:

```ts
import { composeStory } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import meta, { ReactiveValue as ReactiveValueStory } from './style.stories.js'

const ReactiveValue = composeStory(ReactiveValueStory, meta)
```

The project annotations and the export name are the optional third and fourth arguments. The export name sets the `storyName` and the `id` of the composed story; `composeStories` passes it by itself.

## Project Annotations

The decorators, parameters, args, globals and loaders of `.storybook/preview.ts` reach a composed story when the preview is passed to the call: as the second argument of `composeStories`, or as the third of `composeStory`. With the theme preview of Writing Stories, the composed stories get the injection context it opens:

```ts title="src/themed.spec.ts"
import { it, expect } from 'vitest'
import { composeStories } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { render } from '@nanoviews/testing-library'
import preview from '../.storybook/preview.js'
import * as Stories from './themed.stories.js'

const { Default, Dark } = composeStories(Stories, preview)

it('should take the theme from the preview decorator', () => {
  const { container } = render(Default())

  expect(container.innerHTML).toBe('<div><span>light</span></div>')
})

it('should take the globals of the story', () => {
  const { container } = render(Dark())

  expect(container.innerHTML).toBe('<div><span>dark</span></div>')
})
```

Both stories render a component that injects `Theme$`, and `Dark` pins `theme: 'dark'` in its `globals`. Without the preview, there is no context to inject from, and the render throws.

To give the preview to every composed story of a test run instead, call `setProjectAnnotations` once in a setup file, the one of the Vitest config:

```ts title="test/setup.ts"
import { setProjectAnnotations } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import preview from '../.storybook/preview.js'

setProjectAnnotations(preview)
```

Then `composeStories(Stories)` alone gives the stories above the preview, and a preview passed to a call still composes on top of it.

## Loaders

A composed story does not run its loaders by itself. Awaiting its `load()` runs them, and the calls of the story that follow get their result as `context.loaded`. With the `User` story of Writing Stories, and its request mocked:

```ts title="src/user.spec.ts"
import { it, expect, vi } from 'vitest'
import { composeStories } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { render } from '@nanoviews/testing-library'
import * as Stories from './user.stories.js'

vi.mock('./api.js', () => ({
  async fetchUser() {
    return {
      name: 'Ada'
    }
  }
}))

const { Loaded } = composeStories(Stories)

it('should greet the loaded user', async () => {
  await Loaded.load()

  const { container } = render(Loaded())

  expect(container.innerHTML).toBe('<div><p>Hello, Ada</p></div>')
})
```

`vi.mock` swaps `src/api.ts` for the factory before the stories module imports it. Without `load()`, `context.loaded` is an empty object.

Writing Tests covers queries, events, async data and dependency injection in tests, and the API describes the composed story itself, its `play()` and `run()` included.

---

# API

Reference for @nanoviews/storybook and @nanoviews/storybook-vite: the config types, the portable story helpers, the story types and the entry points.

This page describes the public API of `@nanoviews/storybook` and `@nanoviews/storybook-vite`: the config of `.storybook/main.ts`, the portable story helpers, the story types and the entry points.

## `@nanoviews/storybook-vite`

### `StorybookConfig`

The type of the `.storybook/main.ts` default export, as on Getting Started. It is Storybook's own config type from `storybook/internal/types`, extended with the Vite builder option `viteFinal` and changed in two keys:

- `framework` is required: `'@nanoviews/storybook-vite'`, or the [object form](#framework-options). The type suggests the package name to the editor but accepts any string.
- `core.builder` is optional and takes `'@storybook/builder-vite'`, or `{ name, options }` with the builder options. The framework sets the builder already, so it is rarely needed.

Every other key is a [`main.ts` option](https://storybook.js.org/docs/api/main-config/main-config) of Storybook: `stories`, `addons`, `staticDirs`, `docs` and the rest.

### Framework Options

`framework` also accepts the object form, where `options` is a `FrameworkOptions`:

```ts title=".storybook/main.ts"
import type { StorybookConfig } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'

const config: StorybookConfig = {
  framework: {
    name: '@nanoviews/storybook-vite',
    options: {
      builder: {
        viteConfigPath: '.storybook/vite.config.ts'
      }
    }
  },
  stories: ['../src/**/*.stories.ts']
}

export default config
```

`FrameworkOptions` has one key, `builder`, which is optional and passed straight through to [`@storybook/builder-vite`](https://storybook.js.org/docs/builders/vite):

- `viteConfigPath` is the Vite config file to read, resolved relative to `process.cwd()`. By default the builder looks for a `vite.config` file in the project root, the directory that holds `.storybook`.
- `configLoader` is how Vite loads that file: `'bundle'`, `'runner'` or `'native'`, the same as the `--configLoader` flag of Vite. It needs Vite 6.1 or newer and is ignored by older versions.

In the object form `options` is required, so pass `options: {}` when there is nothing to configure.

### `viteFinal`

`StorybookConfig` also types [`viteFinal`](https://storybook.js.org/docs/api/main-config/main-config-vite-final), to extend the resolved Vite config:

```ts title=".storybook/main.ts"
import type { StorybookConfig } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'

const config: StorybookConfig = {
  framework: '@nanoviews/storybook-vite',
  stories: ['../src/**/*.stories.ts'],
  async viteFinal(config) {
    const { mergeConfig } = await import('vite')

    return mergeConfig(config, {
      resolve: {
        alias: {
          '~': '/src'
        }
      }
    })
  }
}

export default config
```

`viteFinal(config, options)` gets the Vite config Storybook resolved and the Storybook options, and returns the config to use, or a promise of it.

### `defineMain`

`@nanoviews/storybook-vite/node` exports `defineMain`, an identity helper that types a `main.ts` config without a type annotation:

```ts title=".storybook/main.ts"
import { defineMain } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite/node'

export default defineMain({
  framework: '@nanoviews/storybook-vite',
  stories: ['../src/**/*.stories.ts']
})
```

### Re-exports

Everything exported by `@nanoviews/storybook` is re-exported from `@nanoviews/storybook-vite`, so a project installs the framework alone and imports its config types and its story types from it.

## `@nanoviews/storybook`

### `composeStories(csfExports, projectAnnotations?)`

Composes all stories of a CSF module, the `import * as Stories` namespace, into callable functions bound to the Nanoviews renderer, and returns them in an object keyed by export name. The meta is the `default` export, and every other export is composed unless the `includeStories` or `excludeStories` of the meta leaves it out. Project annotations, such as the default export of `.storybook/preview.ts`, can be passed as the optional second argument. See Portable Stories.

### `composeStory(story, meta, projectAnnotations?, exportsName?)`

Composes one story into a callable function bound to the Nanoviews renderer. Takes the story object and the meta of its module; project annotations and the export name of the story are the optional third and fourth arguments. The export name gives the composed story its name and id.

### Composed Story

What `composeStory` returns, and `composeStories` returns one per story: a function that takes the args and returns the story unbuilt, a `LazyChild` like a component instance, that `render` of `@nanoviews/testing-library` takes and a view takes as a child. Every arg is optional and accepts a plain value or a writable signal; a plain value is wrapped in a new signal on every call, and an arg left out falls back to the `args` below. The function also has the properties of a composed story of Storybook:

- `args` — the args it falls back to, merged from the project annotations, the meta and the story;
- `parameters`, `argTypes`, `globals` and `tags` — the merged annotations;
- `id` and `storyName`;
- `load()` — runs the loaders, and the calls of the story that follow get their result as `context.loaded`;
- `play(context?)` — runs the `play` function of the story on `document.body`, or on the `canvasElement` the context passes; it is `undefined` when the story has no `play`;
- `run(context?)` — runs the loaders, mounts the story into a new `<div>` appended to `document.body` and runs its `play` function. The `<div>` stays in the document until the next `run()` or `load()` of a composed story removes it.

### `setProjectAnnotations(projectAnnotations)`

Stores project annotations, one object or an array of them, globally, together with the annotations of the renderer. Every story composed afterwards by `composeStory` and `composeStories` gets them, and the annotations passed to a call compose on top. Call it once in a test setup file, as Portable Stories shows.

## Types

### `Meta`

`Meta<typeof Component>` or `Meta<Args>`: the metadata of the default export. Parameterize it with the component or with the plain args type; `args` is plain in both cases, and `render` gets signals. With the component form, a prop typed as `Signalish<T>` or `WritableSignal<T>` takes a plain `T` in `args`, a prop that is only a function stays a function, and a prop typed as a plain value makes `component` a type error, since the renderer hands it a signal. See Typing the Meta.

### `StoryObj`

`StoryObj<typeof meta>`: a CSF3 story object. It can also be parameterized with a component or a plain args type directly, instead of with the meta: `StoryObj<{ muted: boolean }>`.

### `StoryFn`

`StoryFn<Component>` or `StoryFn<Args>`: a CSF2 story function. It is a `render` like any other, it gets the args as signals, and its annotations go on the function:

```ts title="src/bold.stories.ts"
import type { Meta, StoryFn } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { b } from 'nanoviews'

const meta: Meta<{
  label: string
}> = {
  title: 'Bold'
}

export default meta

export const Bold: StoryFn<{
  label: string
}> = ({ label }) => b()(label)

Bold.args = {
  label: 'Hello'
}
// <b>Hello</b>
```

### `Decorator`, `Loader`, `StoryContext`

`Decorator<Args>`, `Loader<Args>` and `StoryContext<Args>` are the decorator, loader and story context types of Storybook, bound to the Nanoviews renderer. `Args` defaults to `StrictArgs`, which types every arg as `unknown`.

Parameterize them with the plain args type. A decorator gets the args as signals all the same, see Args in Decorators; a loader gets them as plain values. The loader of the `User` story of Loaders, as a constant of its own:

```ts title="src/loaders.ts"
import type { Loader } from '@nanoviews/storybook-vite'
import { fetchUser } from './api.js'

export const loadUser: Loader<{
  id: number
}> = async ({ args }) => ({
  user: await fetchUser(args.id)
})
```

A meta or a story with the same args takes it in its `loaders`.

### `Preview`

The type of the `.storybook/preview.ts` default export, as on Getting Started.

### Renderer Types

- `NanoviewsRenderer<Props>` is the renderer itself: its `component` takes the signal props, `SignalProps<Props>`, its `storyResult` is the view they render, a `Child`, and its canvas element is an `HTMLElement`.
- `NanoviewsMountRenderer<Props>` is the renderer as seen after `applyDecorators`, which defers the whole decorated story: its `storyResult` is a `LazyChild`, the story unbuilt, instead of a view. A composed story is typed with it.

### Props Types

The types that map the three shapes of a prop into each other:

| Type                   | What it is                            | Example                                                     |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ComponentType<Props>` | a function from props to a view       | `(props: Props) => Child`                                   |
| `ComponentArgs<T>`     | the plain args of a component's props | `{ a: Signalish<number> }` → `{ a: number }`                |
| `SignalProps<T>`       | what `render` gets for plain args     | `{ a: number }` → `{ a: WritableSignal<number> }`           |
| `RawProps<T>`          | signal props back to plain values     | `{ a: WritableSignal<number> }` → `{ a: number }`           |
| `UniversalProps<T>`    | what a composed story accepts         | `{ a: number }` → `{ a: number \| WritableSignal<number> }` |

`ComponentArgs` and `SignalProps` leave a prop that is only a function, like an event handler, as it is, and `SignalProps` and `UniversalProps` keep a signal prop as it is. An optional prop keeps its `undefined` outside the signal (`b?: WritableSignal<string>`), while a required prop that takes `undefined` holds it inside (`WritableSignal<string | undefined>`).

### Storybook Types

`Args`, `ArgTypes`, `Parameters` and `StrictArgs` are re-exported from `storybook/internal/types`.

## Entry Points

| Entry point                          | Exports                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@nanoviews/storybook`               | `composeStories`, `composeStory`, `setProjectAnnotations` and the types above.                                                                                                                                   |
| `@nanoviews/storybook/preset`        | `previewAnnotations`, the Storybook preset hook that adds the preview entry below to the config. `@nanoviews/storybook-vite` points at it as `core.renderer`; a framework for another builder would do the same. |
| `@nanoviews/storybook/entry-preview` | The preview annotations of the renderer: `parameters`, `applyDecorators`, `render`, `renderToCanvas` and `argTypesEnhancers`.                                                                                    |
| `@nanoviews/storybook-vite`          | `StorybookConfig`, `FrameworkOptions` and every export of `@nanoviews/storybook`.                                                                                                                                |
| `@nanoviews/storybook-vite/node`     | `defineMain`.                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `@nanoviews/storybook-vite/preset`   | The framework preset, `core`: the builder, `@storybook/builder-vite`, and the renderer, `@nanoviews/storybook/preset`.                                                                                           |

Storybook loads the presets and the preview entry by itself once `framework` names `@nanoviews/storybook-vite`: a project imports none of them. What the preview annotations do with a story is described in Args Are Signals.
